summary: Paul and other prisoners sail for Italy under the centurion Julius, with Aristarchus and the first-person narrator present. After changing ships and fighting contrary winds, they reach Fair Havens after the Fast, when the voyage has become dangerous. Paul warns that continuing risks cargo, ship, and lives, but the centurion trusts the pilot and owner. A violent northeaster drives the ship for two weeks; cargo and tackle are thrown overboard and hope disappears. Paul reports an angelic promise that he must stand before Caesar and that God has graciously given him all aboard. He insists that sailors remain with the ship, urges all 276 people to eat, gives thanks and breaks bread, and guides them through wreck on the shore of an island (named Malta in 28:1). Soldiers plan to kill prisoners, but Julius preserves Paul and everyone reaches land alive.
whyItMatters: The voyage is told with many technical sailing details and turns a prisoner into the ship's moral center without making expertise irrelevant. Paul warns, receives promise, tells the truth, prevents abandonment, nourishes exhausted people, and trusts God while sailors sound depths and cut anchors. Providence works through competent action, and salvation includes every person aboard—not only the famous apostle.

context.author: The anonymous first-person Luke–Acts narrator, traditionally Luke, Paul's companion, reporting Paul's voyage toward Rome
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider audience that knows Israel's Greek Scriptures; here, readers accompanying the promised witness through technical danger, imperial custody, and communal survival
context.date: Acts is often dated around AD 80–90, though some argue for the 60s or later; the voyage sets out after the Fast (27:9), with winter near (27:12)
context.setting: Sidon, Cyprus, Myra, Cnidus, Crete, the Adriatic Sea, and an island named as Malta in 28:1
context.literaryForm: Ancient sea-voyage and storm narrative with prophecy, meal, wreck, and rescue

outline.heading: The prisoners sail under Julius and reach Fair Havens with difficulty
outline.note: The centurion Julius takes Paul and other prisoners by ship, treats Paul kindly at Sidon, and contrary winds slow them to Fair Havens

outline.heading: Paul's warning is rejected and a northeaster overwhelms the ship
outline.note: Paul warns of loss, but the centurion heeds the ship's master; a stormy wind drives them, and all hope of being saved is gone

outline.heading: Paul announces preservation and prevents the sailors' escape
outline.note: Paul says an angel stood by him and no life will be lost; when sailors try to flee, soldiers cut the boat's ropes

outline.heading: All eat, the ship wrecks, and every person reaches land
outline.note: Paul urges all to eat and breaks bread with thanks; the ship runs aground and the stern breaks up, but all reach land

keyVerses.text: For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve,
keyVerses.why: Paul's identity is expressed as belonging and service within imperial captivity and natural danger.

keyVerses.text: Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.
keyVerses.why: Faith means trusting the promise while still following concrete survival measures.

keyVerses.text: Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.”
keyVerses.why: Salvation is bodily and communal: exhausted people need food in order to survive.

questions.question: Why does the narration return to ‘we’?
questions.answer: The first-person plural resumes at departure and includes the narrator among those sailing, suffering, eating, and surviving. It may be direct participant memory, a travel source, or literary voyage convention; its dense nautical detail strengthens the impression of proximity but still does not name the narrator. Aristarchus is separately identified as companion.

questions.question: Who is Julius, and why does he matter?
questions.answer: He is a centurion of the ‘Augustan band’ (27:1). He treats Paul kindly at Sidon, initially follows maritime experts rather than Paul's warning, later listens about the sailors, and finally prevents prisoner execution. Roman authority is personal and changeable, capable of both custody and preservation.

questions.question: What is ‘the Fast,’ and why is sailing dangerous afterward?
questions.answer: ‘The Fast’ most naturally means the Day of Atonement, kept in the seventh month (Leviticus 23:27), after which, the text says, sailing was dangerous and winter near (27:9, 12). Luke uses a Jewish calendar marker within a Roman voyage. The timing explains Paul's warning without requiring his first advice to be supernatural prophecy.

questions.question: Is Paul contradicting the angel when he says sailors must stay aboard?
questions.answer: The promise says all lives will be given to Paul and the ship will be lost; later Paul says the passengers cannot be saved unless the sailors remain. Promise and means cooperate: skilled crew are part of how preservation occurs. Trust in God does not justify sabotaging the ordinary actions the situation requires.

questions.question: What does Paul mean by ‘God has granted you all those who sail with you’?
questions.answer: Kecharistai comes from the grace/gift family: God has graciously given the lives of Paul's shipmates in connection with the promise that he must reach Caesar. This does not make people Paul's property. It portrays intercessory, representative preservation radiating through a prisoner whom the empire treats as disposable.

questions.question: Is the bread-breaking meal a Eucharist?
questions.answer: Paul takes bread, gives thanks to God before all, breaks it, and eats—language that echoes the Last Supper (Luke 22:19). It is also plainly a practical shipboard meal needed after prolonged fasting. Luke can let sacred resonance and ordinary nourishment inhabit the same act; the whole mixed company eats, while no formal liturgy is described.

questions.question: Why specify 276 people?
questions.answer: The exact total underscores the scale of the ship and allows the final ‘all’ to be concrete. Codex Vaticanus reads ‘about seventy-six,’ but most witnesses read 276. Large Alexandrian grain ships could carry hundreds, so the figure is not inherently implausible.

questions.question: How reliable is Acts' nautical terminology?
questions.answer: The chapter uses numerous precise terms for winds, undergirding, sea anchor, sounding, anchors, rudder bands, foresail, shoal, and stern breakup. Scholars debate reconstructing the exact route and modern equivalences for rare words, but the language displays real familiarity with ancient Mediterranean sailing rather than generic storm scenery.

questions.question: Why do soldiers plan to kill the prisoners?
questions.answer: Guards in Acts could pay with their lives for escaped prisoners (12:19; 16:27), so death prevents escape during the wreck. Julius wants to save Paul and stops the plan, thereby saving all prisoners as well. The scene exposes how imperial procedure can treat captive lives as risk liabilities even at the moment of common disaster.

glossary.def: Usually taken as the Day of Atonement, kept in the seventh month (Leviticus 23:27); here a calendar marker for dangerous sailing.
A violent northeaster, also called Euraquilo in textual traditions, that drives the ship.
Measuring water depth, here in fathoms, to detect approaching land.
